newsitem.title: USA: Scientists eye future of AIDS therapies.
newsitem.headline: Scientists eye future of AIDS therapies.

text.p: AIDS researchers gathering for a major conference starting on Wednesday said the latest data reinforces optimism about improved therapies but leaves open the question of whether doctors are close to a cure.

Dr. David Ho, perhaps the world's best-known AIDS researcher, said he has decided not to take any of his patients off the new drug combination therapies after only a year to test whether they have been cured.
He said, however, he believes such an experiment may still be possible after 24 to 30 months on the new drugs.
"Can HIV be eradicated? We don't know," Ho told reporters at a briefing before the Fourth Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections formally convened.
"No patient so far as far as I know has been cured," said Ho, of the Aaron Diamond AIDS Research Centre in New York. "It's justified to feel some degree of optimism. But we have a long way to go."

New drugs, including a category known as protease inhibitors, have suppressed the virus to undetectable levels in some patients. If the virus cannot reproduce, theoretically it may eventually die out as the cells it has infected die.

Ho said a combination of clinical studies on his patients' blood, semen and lymph tissue and his mathematical models indicate it would take 24 to 30 months for the virus to clear out of the cells now known to store it. He had earlier contemplated stopping therapy after 12 months.
However, he stressed that there may be other unknown "compartments" of infection in the human body, which could harbour the virus and let it rebound if medication is halted.

Ho also said his team had found that the virus could not be detected in his patients' semen. That is encouraging in terms of reducing the spread of AIDS through sex but he emphasised there was not enough information yet to draw any conclusions or to undercut the importance of safe sex messages.

Dr. Peter Piot, the head of the Geneva-based U.N. AIDS programme, noted that 90 percent of the 30 million people who have been infected with the virus live in poor countries, where expensive multi-drug therapies are out of reach.
He pleaded for more research on tools to prevent AIDS, particularly a vaccine.

Over the next five days 2,100 researchers at the conference will look at data on the new treatments and attempt to figure out which hopes may be fulfilled and which may yield to harsh reality about how tough it is to vanquish the lethal virus that has claimed 6.5 million lives.

There is no doubt the new drug combinations are transforming and prolonging the lives of many AIDS patients, particularly those who start therapy soon after becoming infected. Thousands of them feel well, look well and are living lives that they feared would have been over by now.
But not everyone succeeds on the drugs and there have been some reports of problems with resistance, where strains of HIV may be becoming impervious to the new therapies.
"For the majority of our patients the response to treatment has been fantastic," said Dr. Peter Ruane, who treats AIDS patients and conducts research in Los Angeles.
"But like everybody else, we do not know how long these treatments will be effective. We're very worried about resistance -- that's what it's all about," Ruane said in an interview.

Since so many new drugs became available so fast, some doctors have been uncertain how to best use them. The conference will look at the specific combinations, as well as some of the successes in treating so-called opportunistic infections, diseases that afflict and kill AIDS patients.
